decision.explanation: T(x,y)=(-2x-y,4x+2y). The vertices (0,1), (1,0), and (2,2) map to (-1,2), (-2,4), and (-6,12). These points lie on y=-2x, so the triangle maps to the line segment from (-6,12) to (-1,2), shown in option d.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073713/assets/db7d2b33f2badad28b754d4482047a33bb37469ed8b7b17859b10552840e2f51.png)

Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Which of the following is the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$
after.worked_solution:
To find the image of the triangle under the action of $T$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of the triangle:

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the action of $T$ by calculating the matrix product $TX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -6 & -1 \\ 4 & 12 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the image's vertices are $(-2,4)$, 
$(-6,12)$ and $(-1,2).$ Notice that all three points lie on the same line.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073713/assets/2e1dde461c6244a59672fc28c842b70a30297ac7a8c7e7cf2095a973cd1860cd.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073713/assets/e2ab6906100a96a123b4b1520613f1e38fe2c7e77af390a8efe0596a2861727d.png)

Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

What would be the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any linear transformation $T$ with associated $2\times 2$ matrix $T,$ we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., $det(T)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., $det(T)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $T$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $T$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is the point $(0,0),$ the origin of the coordinate system.

Since $T$ is the zero matrix, the image of our object under the action of $T$ is the origin.

history.worked_solution:
Recall that for any linear transformation $T$ with associated $2\times 2$ matrix $T,$ we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., $det(T)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., $det(T)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $T$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $T$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is the point $(0,0),$ the origin of the coordinate system.

Since $T$ is the zero matrix, the image of our object under the action of $T$ is the origin.
